name: Prague
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: The Czech capital on the Vltava, a spired 'City of a Hundred Towers' that came through WWII almost intact. T1: on the Old Town Square, every hour a crowd gathers as the Orloj (Astronomical Clock) puts on its show -- two little doors open and the Twelve Apostles parade past while a carved skeleton (Death) rings a bell and flips his hourglass (answer = the parading Apostle figures / the moving skeleton). T2: invert the wonder -- that clock, first recorded in 1410, is over 600 years old, the world's OLDEST astronomical clock still running (the huge age is the hook; 'oldest still-working astronomical clock' is the answer). T2: Golden Lane inside Prague Castle is a row of tiny candy-colored cottages built INTO the castle wall for Rudolf II's guards, later home to the goldsmiths that gave it its name (answer = Golden Lane / the goldsmiths). T3: Charles Bridge, begun in 1357 under Charles IV, is lined with 30 blackened baroque statues of saints -- the most-rubbed is St John of Nepomuk (answer = the 30 saint statues). T3: legend says the bridge's masons mixed egg yolks (even eggs shipped in from whole villages) into the mortar to harden it -- and modern lab tests really did find organic binders in it (answer = eggs in the mortar; label as legend that testing partly confirmed). T4: St Vitus Cathedral, rising inside the castle, was begun in 1344 and not finished until 1929 -- nearly 600 years under construction (answer = ~600 years to build). T4: Prague Castle is often called the largest coherent ancient castle complex in the world, spreading over roughly 70,000 square metres above the river (answer = largest ancient castle complex). T5: in the 1618 Defenestration of Prague, angry Protestants threw two royal officials (and a secretary) out a high Prague Castle window -- and all three SURVIVED the ~20 m fall, landing in the moat below (legend says a dung heap broke their fall); the event helped ignite the Thirty Years' War (answer = they survived the fall).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Prague astronomical clock', 'Charles Bridge', 'List of statues on Charles Bridge', 'Golden Lane'; prague.eu (Prague City Tourism, Old Town Hall/Orloj, Charles Bridge); Britannica 'Prague Castle'; charlesbridgehostel.com (egg-mortar lab tests). Grokipedia checked for Prague sights.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led, place is always visible in the stem ('on the Old Town Square...', 'inside Prague Castle...'). Accuracy rail: the egg-mortar and the dung-heap survival are LEGEND that some evidence supports -- word them as legend/tradition, not flat fact; the clock is the world's THIRD-oldest astronomical clock overall but the OLDEST still operating (state it precisely so a distractor 'the very first astronomical clock ever built' stays wrong-but-adjacent). Distractors = other real European clocks/bridges/castles. Dinner-test payoff: the Defenestration survivors landing in a dung heap (T5). Keep answers PLACE-anchored: the clock rung's answer is the parading figures, not 'what time it shows'.
history_overlap: The 1618 Defenestration as the CAUSE of the Thirty Years' War is a history-bank episode; keep this geography rung's answer on the vivid place-fact (three men survived a fall from a Prague Castle window), not on the war's diplomacy or outcome.

name: Vienna
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: The Habsburg imperial capital on the Danube, the 'City of Music'. T1: at the Prater fairground the giant red Ferris wheel (the Riesenrad), built in 1897, turns slowly over the city -- one of the world's oldest, and for decades the tallest Ferris wheel on Earth (answer = the Riesenrad / long the world's tallest). T2: the WALTZ -- the whirling close-hold three-step dance -- was born in Vienna's ballrooms and was once banned as scandalously improper until the Congress of Vienna (1814-15) made it respectable; Johann Strauss II, the 'Waltz King', turned it into the city's signature (answer = the waltz, born in Vienna's ballrooms). T2: Viennese coffee-house culture is so distinctive that UNESCO listed it as 'intangible cultural heritage' in 2011 -- one small coffee buys a marble table for hours, with newspapers clipped on wooden frames (answer = the coffee house, a UNESCO cultural treasure). T3: the Ringstrasse -- Emperor Franz Joseph in 1857 ordered the old medieval city walls torn DOWN and replaced with a grand tree-lined boulevard ringed by monumental buildings (answer = the boulevard built where the city walls once stood). T3: at the Central Cemetery (Zentralfriedhof), a cluster of honorary graves holds Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms and Strauss side by side -- yet Mozart isn't really there: he has only a monument, his true grave lost in an unmarked pauper's plot across town (answer = the composers' graves / Mozart's grave is lost). T4: the Spanish Riding School in the Hofburg, founded in 1572, is the world's OLDEST classical dressage academy still running, where white Lipizzaner stallions perform leaps called 'airs above the ground' (answer = the school / oldest riding academy). T4: the Hofburg palace was the winter seat of the Habsburg dynasty for over 600 years, the heart of an empire (answer = the Habsburg palace). T5: Vienna is the 'City of Music' because Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven all lived and worked within its walls -- the birthplace of what's called the First Viennese School (answer = Vienna, home of the great classical composers).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Wiener Riesenrad', 'Spanish Riding School'; wien.info / austria.info (official Vienna tourism: Viennese waltz, coffeehouse culture UNESCO 2011, Ringstrasse); visitingvienna.com (Riesenrad, Zentralfriedhof composers).
framing_note: Voice: the CREATION born in the place is the wonder (the waltz, the coffee house) -- Vienna is always the anchor in the stem. Accuracy rail: state the waltz was 'popularized/made respectable' at the Congress of Vienna, not literally invented in one night; the coffee-house UNESCO listing is 2011, the waltz listing 2017 -- keep them distinct so a swapped-date distractor stays wrong. Dinner-test payoff: Mozart's grave being LOST while lesser names lie in honor (T3). LANE BORDER: the Lipizzaner is a horse -- its biology (foals born dark, coats turning white by age 6-10) belongs to the ANIMAL bank; keep this rung's answer the PLACE/institution (the 450-year-old riding school in the Hofburg), a one-line horse mention at most.

name: St Petersburg
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Russia's imperial 'Venice of the North', raised on the Neva delta. T1: for weeks around midsummer the city glows through the 'White Nights' -- the sun barely sets and the sky never goes fully dark, so people fill the streets and bridges past midnight (answer = the White Nights). T2: Peter the Great founded the city in 1703 by sheer decree on a cold, mist-shrouded MARSH at the mouth of the Neva -- tens of thousands of laborers drained swamp and drove wooden piles, and so many died it's called 'the city built on bones' (answer = built on a drained marsh, by decree). T2: over 60 rivers and canals thread across more than 40 islands, crossed by hundreds of bridges -- earning it the name 'Venice of the North' (answer = the canal-and-island city / Venice of the North). T3: invert the wonder -- the Hermitage, spread through the green-and-white Winter Palace, holds around three million objects, making it the world's SECOND-largest art museum (the vast collection is the hook; 'second-largest art museum' the answer); it grew from Catherine the Great's 1764 purchase. T3: every night in shipping season the Neva's drawbridges rise to let ocean ships pass -- and if you're caught on the wrong bank, you're stranded until dawn (answer = the drawbridges open at night). T4: at Peterhof, Peter's seaside palace, more than 100 fountains including the Grand Cascade run with NO pumps at all -- gravity alone drives the water down from springs and reservoirs about 20 km away (answer = the gravity-fed fountains, no pumps). T4: the Bronze Horseman statue of Peter rears on the 'Thunder Stone' -- a single granite boulder of roughly 1,500 tonnes, among the largest stones ever moved by people, hauled to the city over a track of bronze balls (answer = the Thunder Stone / a giant moved boulder). T5: the city sits so far north (about 60 degrees N) that the Neva freezes solid every winter and the summer sun scarcely dips -- its polar-edge latitude shapes the whole rhythm of the year (answer = its far-north latitude).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Saint Petersburg', 'Hermitage Museum', 'Peterhof Palace', 'List of bridges in Saint Petersburg'; introducingsaintpetersburg.com (Hermitage, history); russiable.com (drawbridge schedules); go.peterhofmuseum.ru (gravity fountains). Grokipedia checked.
framing_note: Voice: the PLACE and its earth/engineering are the wonder; invert on the Hermitage (millions of objects -> second-largest). Accuracy rail: the human cost of building on the marsh is real -- state it plainly and honestly (thousands of forced laborers died) without turning it into a lecture; the Hermitage is second-largest by GALLERY SPACE/collection, so keep a 'largest art museum in the world' (the Louvre) as a live wrong-but-adjacent distractor. Dinner-test payoff: Peterhof's fountains running for 300 years on gravity alone (T4). Keep answers place-anchored, not a bare 'Peter the Great' name.
history_overlap: Peter the Great's westernizing reforms and the Great Northern War are history-bank material; keep the founding rung's answer on the SITE fact (a capital willed into being on a drained Neva marsh), not on Peter's policies.

name: Moscow
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Russia's capital on the Moskva, gathered around the Kremlin. T1: Red Square gets its name from an old Russian word 'krasnaya', which once meant 'beautiful' -- not the color red and nothing to do with communism; it is really the 'Beautiful Square' (answer = 'red' once meant 'beautiful'; teach the word before testing). T2: on the square stands St Basil's Cathedral, built for Ivan the Terrible in 1555-61 to mark the conquest of Kazan -- nine separate chapels fused into one, topped with candy-swirl onion domes each painted differently (answer = St Basil's, nine churches in one; the tale that Ivan blinded the architects is apocryphal -- label as legend). T2: the Kremlin itself is a great triangular fortress of red-brick walls and 20 towers, still the seat of Russian power and one of the largest active medieval fortresses in Europe (answer = the Kremlin fortress). T3: the Moscow Metro was built as 'palaces for the people' -- stations like Komsomolskaya hung with chandeliers, faced in marble, and roofed with mosaics of Russian war heroes (answer = the palace-stations). T4: invert the wonder -- Park Pobedy station lies about 84 m underground, Moscow's DEEPEST, reached by one of Europe's longest escalators at roughly 126 m (the extreme depth is the hook; 'the deepest station' the answer). T4: GUM, the grand glass-roofed shopping arcade, runs the whole east side of Red Square like an indoor street of iron and glass (answer = the GUM arcade). T5: many metro stations were dug so deep on purpose -- they doubled as bomb shelters, and during WWII thousands sheltered underground, with a command post built into one station (answer = the metro as bomb shelter).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Grokipedia 'Park Pobedy (Moscow Metro)'; Wikipedia 'Saint Basil's Cathedral', 'Red Square', 'Moscow Metro', 'Komsomolskaya (Koltsevaya line)'; rbth.com / rusmania.com (metro stations); worldatlas.com (deepest stations).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led, Moscow landmark always named. Accuracy rail: label the 'Ivan blinded the architects' story as popular legend (almost certainly untrue); the 'Red Square = Beautiful Square' etymology must be TAUGHT in the stem's setup enough to be fair but the answer still requires knowing which meaning is original. Be factually honest about the metro: a genuine engineering marvel AND a Soviet showpiece built under Stalin. Dinner-test payoff: Park Pobedy 84 m down with a 126 m escalator (T4). Distractors = other real deep metros / other onion-domed churches.
history_overlap: The Kremlin as the seat of Tsarist/Soviet/modern political power invites history-bank episodes; keep these rungs on the PLACE (the fortress walls, the domes, the deep stations), not on regimes or leaders' deeds.

name: Athens
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: The birthplace of Western civic life, crowned by its sacred rock. T1: the Acropolis (Greek for 'high city') is a flat-topped rock rising about 150 m over Athens, a natural citadel you can see from almost anywhere in the city, its summit crowned with ancient temples (answer = the Acropolis, the high citadel-rock; teach 'acropolis'). T2: on top stands the Parthenon (447-432 BC), the temple of Athena, built of gleaming Pentelic marble that weathers to a warm honey-gold in the sun (answer = the Parthenon / marble that turns golden). T3: the Parthenon has almost NO straight lines -- its columns swell slightly in the middle (entasis) and lean inward, and the floor curves gently up in the center -- deliberate optical tricks so the temple LOOKS perfectly straight to the eye (answer = the built-in curves / optical refinements; teach entasis). T3: the Agora, the open marketplace at the foot of the rock, was the civic heart of Athens -- where citizens gathered to trade, vote and argue, and where Socrates buttonholed passersby with questions (answer = the Agora, the civic marketplace). T4: on the Erechtheion's 'Porch of the Maidens', six carved stone women (the Caryatids) stand in place of columns, holding the roof on their heads (answer = the Caryatids). T4: all that marble came from Mount Pentelicus, northeast of the city -- roughly 13,000 blocks of Pentelic marble quarried and hauled up onto the rock (answer = quarried from Mt Pentelicus). T5: the Parthenon stood nearly whole for over 2,000 years until 1687, when a Venetian cannon-shell struck Ottoman gunpowder stored inside and blew the roof and center apart in an instant (answer = a 1687 gunpowder explosion wrecked it).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Acropolis of Athens', 'Parthenon'; Britannica 'Parthenon', 'Acropolis of Athens'; UNESCO WHC list #404 (Acropolis); archeyes.com / thearchaeologist.org (optical refinements, entasis, stylobate curvature).
framing_note: Voice: PLACE -> WONDER, the rock and its marble are the stars; invert nothing that turns it into a definition-shell -- lead with the scene ('on top of the rock stands...'). Accuracy rail: keep the optical-refinement numbers loose in the seed (the stylobate rises a few cm at center; columns lean inward) and let the build research nail exacts; the 1687 explosion is a well-documented event, state it as fact. Dinner-test payoff: the temple with no straight lines that only LOOKS straight (T3). LANE BORDER: Socrates' trial, execution and ideas belong to the history/philosophy banks -- this Agora rung's answer is the PLACE (the marketplace that was the city's civic heart), Socrates a one-line mention.
history_overlap: Socrates (trial/philosophy) and Pericles' Golden Age are history/philosophy episodes; the 1687 Morosini bombardment is a history event -- keep every rung's answer a PLACE fact (the rock, the marble, the Agora, the ruin's cause) rather than a person or a war.

name: Budapest
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Hungary's capital astride the Danube, the 'City of Spas'. T1: Budapest is really TWO old towns joined into one -- hilly, castle-topped Buda on the west bank and flat, bustling Pest on the east, first linked by the Chain Bridge in 1849 (answer = Buda + Pest, split by the Danube; teach the two halves). T2: invert the wonder -- more than 100 natural hot springs bubble up beneath the city, more than any other capital, which is why it's called the 'City of Spas' (the 100+ springs are the hook; 'the thermal springs' the answer). T2: the Szechenyi Baths, a lemon-yellow palace of a bathhouse, is the LARGEST medicinal bath in Europe, fed by a spring drilled 1,256 m down that comes up at 77 degrees C -- in winter people play chess in the steaming outdoor pools while snow falls (answer = Szechenyi, Europe's largest medicinal bath). T3: all that hot water rises through a huge maze of THERMAL CAVES hollowed in the limestone under the Buda hills -- one of the largest thermal-water cave systems in the world (answer = the thermal cave system; teach that warm water dissolves limestone into caves). T3: the springs exist because Budapest sits right on a geological FAULT line, where the Buda hills meet the Pest plain and deep-warmed water can rise to the surface (answer = a fault line lets the hot water up). T4: beneath Buda Castle hill runs a labyrinth of caves and cellars cut into the soft limestone, used over the centuries as shelters, storerooms and even a wartime hospital (answer = the castle-hill cave labyrinth). T4: the Hungarian Parliament on the Pest riverbank is one of the largest parliament buildings in the world, its neo-Gothic spires doubled in the Danube at night (answer = the Parliament building).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Szechenyi thermal bath', 'Spas in Budapest'; Lonely Planet (Budapest thermal baths guide); National Geographic (Hungary thermal spas); bathsbudapest.com.
framing_note: Voice: the earth-process (geothermal water rising through karst) IS the wonder and the place is named in every stem. Accuracy rail: keep the spring count as 'over 100' (sources vary 80-123) and the Szechenyi spring figures exact (1,256 m, 77 C); teach that hot mineral water dissolving limestone makes the cave network (karst) before leaning on it. Dinner-test payoff: chess players in a steaming outdoor pool in the snow (T2). LANE BORDER: this is the PLACE's geothermal geology -- no spa 'health cure' claims stated as medical fact.

name: Krakow
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Poland's old royal capital on the Vistula, a medieval city that survived the war. T1: beneath Wawel Hill yawns a real cave, the 'Dragon's Den' (Smocza Jama), where legend says the fire-breathing Wawel Dragon once lived -- and a bronze dragon at the cave mouth still puffs real fire for visitors (answer = the Dragon's Den cave; label the dragon as legend). T2: that cave is a natural KARST cavern -- limestone slowly dissolved by groundwater into a chain of corridors and chambers about 80 m long under the castle hill (answer = a karst limestone cave; teach karst). T2: Krakow's Old Town came through WWII almost untouched while Warsaw and most Polish cities were flattened -- leaving one of Europe's best-preserved medieval centers (answer = it survived the war nearly intact). T3: invert the wonder -- the Main Market Square (Rynek Glowny), laid out in 1257 with each side over 200 m long, is the LARGEST medieval town square in Europe (the huge open square is the hook; 'largest medieval square' the answer). T3: right in the middle of that square stands the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice), a long Renaissance market hall where merchants have traded cloth and goods for some 700 years (answer = the Cloth Hall). T4: every hour a live trumpeter plays the 'hejnal' from the tower of St Mary's Basilica -- and the tune BREAKS OFF abruptly mid-note, said to honor a medieval watchman shot in the throat as he sounded the alarm (answer = the trumpet call cut off mid-note; label the arrow as legend). T4: Wawel Castle crowns the hill as the old coronation seat of Polish kings, and in the cathedral doorway hang giant 'dragon bones' -- really a whale bone and a mammoth bone -- long believed to protect the city (answer = the 'dragon bones' / really whale and mammoth bones; legend).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Wawel Dragon', 'Main Square, Krakow', 'St. Mary's Trumpet Call'; krakow.travel (hejnal, market square); inyourpocket.com (Wawel dragon, dragon bones).
framing_note: Voice: place-anchored wonder, Krakow/Wawel named in the stem. Accuracy rail: the dragon, the arrow-in-the-throat and the protective bones are LEGEND -- word them as legend/oral tradition, with the sober fact (the cave is real karst; the 'dragon bones' are actually whale and mammoth bones) as the answer where possible. Dinner-test payoff: the hourly trumpet that stops mid-note for a slain medieval watchman (T4). Distractors = other real Polish/European squares, caves, towers.

name: Wieliczka Salt Mine
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: A satellite gem just outside Krakow: a 700-year-old salt mine turned underground cathedral. T1: below the town of Wieliczka near Krakow, miners dug salt for some 700 years (from the 13th century until 1996) -- and deep in the tunnels they carved an entire CHAPEL, St Kinga's Chapel, out of the rock itself: altar, statues, staircases and even the floor tiles (answer = the underground salt chapel). T2: everything that glitters in that chapel is SALT -- the 'crystal' chandeliers, the carved reliefs of Bible scenes, the altar -- all cut by miners from grey, faintly see-through rock salt; lick a wall and it tastes of salt (answer = it is all carved from rock salt). T3: the mine chases a thick bed of rock salt left behind when an ancient sea slowly dried up and evaporated long ago -- following it, miners hollowed out passages reaching 327 m deep and stretching over 287 km underground (answer = salt from a dried-up ancient sea / an evaporite bed).
source: WebFetch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Wieliczka Salt Mine' -- confirmed: operated ~700 years (13th c. to 1996), depth 327 m, over 287 km of passages, chapels and statues carved by miners from rock salt.
framing_note: Voice: the wonder is that a mine became a cathedral of salt -- Wieliczka named in the stem. Accuracy rail: depth (327 m) and passage length (287 km) are Wikipedia-confirmed; the geological detail 'an ancient sea dried up' is the general (true) mechanism for a rock-salt/evaporite bed -- the build's research should confirm the exact Miocene age (~13-14 million years) before stating a number, so seed it as 'an ancient sea that evaporated' not a hard date. Dinner-test payoff: a full cathedral -- chandeliers and all -- carved from salt (T1). Note: this is a distinct site near Krakow, not part of the city proper; kept as a mini because it is a canonical UNESCO geography wonder.

name: Stockholm
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Sweden's capital, a city floating on water. T1: Stockholm is built across 14 islands, right where the freshwater Lake Malaren pours into the salty Baltic Sea, all stitched together by around 50 bridges (answer = a city spread over 14 islands). T2: invert the wonder -- those 14 are only the start: beyond the city the Stockholm Archipelago scatters outward into roughly 30,000 islands, islets and bare rock skerries (the staggering island count is the hook; 'the 30,000-island archipelago' the answer). T2: Gamla Stan, the old town crowded onto one small island, is one of Europe's best-preserved medieval city cores -- a knot of narrow lanes and ochre houses around the Royal Palace (answer = Gamla Stan, the medieval island core). T3: the Vasa, a towering royal warship, capsized and SANK right in Stockholm harbor in 1628 -- barely 1,300 m into her maiden voyage -- because she was built far too tall and heavy with cannon and rolled over in a light gust (answer = she sank on her maiden voyage). T4: the cold, low-salt Baltic water kept out the wood-eating shipworms, so when the Vasa was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom, about 98% of her was still original oak -- now standing whole in her own museum (answer = raised 98% intact after 333 years). T4: the Stockholm Metro is called the 'world's longest art gallery' -- more than 90 stations painted, sculpted or blasted straight into the bare bedrock, like T-Centralen's cave-like blue vines (answer = the metro art gallery).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Vasa (ship)', 'Vasa Museum', 'Geography of Stockholm'; visitstockholm.com ('world's longest art gallery' metro); dailyscandinavian.com (14 islands).
framing_note: Voice: PLACE and its water-geography lead; invert on the archipelago (14 islands -> 30,000). Accuracy rail: the Baltic-preservation science is the real reason the Vasa survived (brackish, low-oxygen water blocks shipworm) -- state it as the mechanism, ~98% original wood; keep '1628 sank / 1961 raised / 333 years' exact so a swapped-number distractor stays wrong. Dinner-test payoff: a 17th-century warship pulled up almost whole after 333 years (T4). LANE BORDER: the shipworm is an animal -- name it only as the agent the Baltic water excludes; the answer stays the PLACE/preservation fact.

name: Reykjavik
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Iceland's capital, the city the earth heats. T1: invert the wonder -- Reykjavik sits at about 64 degrees N, near the Arctic Circle, making it the world's NORTHERNMOST capital of a sovereign country (the extreme latitude is the hook; 'northernmost capital' the answer). T2: almost the whole city is warmed straight from the ground -- nearly every home is heated by naturally hot GEOTHERMAL water piped up from volcanic rock, so Reykjavik burns almost no oil or coal for heat and its air stays clean (answer = geothermal district heating). T2: the city's very name says it -- 'Reykjavik' means 'Smoky Bay', for the plumes of steam the first Norse settlers saw drifting up from the hot springs (answer = the name means 'Smoky Bay'; teach before testing). T3: Hallgrimskirkja, the great pale church towering on the hill, was designed to look like Iceland's BASALT COLUMNS -- the natural hexagonal rock pillars that form when thick lava cools slowly (answer = shaped like basalt columns; teach basalt). T4: Reykjavik lies so far north that midsummer brings a near-endless 'midnight sun' that barely sets, while midwinter gives only a few hours of dim daylight (answer = the midnight sun and dark winters).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Hellisheidi Power Station' (Reykjavik ~90% geothermal district heating); guidetoiceland.is (Hallgrimskirkja basalt-column design); lifeinnorway.net ('14 Facts About Reykjavik', northernmost capital, Smoky Bay).
framing_note: Voice: the earth-process (a city heated by volcanic ground) IS the wonder; Reykjavik named every stem. Accuracy rail: precise wording -- 'northernmost capital of a SOVEREIGN state' (so Nuuk, Greenland, a non-sovereign capital, is a live wrong-but-adjacent distractor); ~90% of Reykjavik buildings use geothermal district heat, so say 'nearly all', not 'all'. Teach 'basalt' before the Hallgrimskirkja rung. Dinner-test payoff: a whole capital heated by hot water straight from the ground (T2). Distractors = other far-north capitals / other volcanic-island facts.

name: Tallinn
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Estonia's capital, a medieval walled town that still works. T1: Tallinn's Old Town is a fairy-tale medieval city that people still live and work in -- cobbled lanes, red-tiled roofs, and a ring of stone walls topped with pointed watchtowers (answer = the intact walled medieval town). T2: invert the wonder -- of the town wall's original 46 towers, about half still stand, making it one of the best-preserved medieval city walls in northern Europe (the surviving array of towers is the hook; 'the medieval town wall' the answer). T2: the town has an upstairs and a downstairs: Toompea, the upper town perched on a limestone hill for nobles, clergy and rulers (Estonia's parliament sits there today), and the merchants' lower town below (answer = Toompea, the upper town on the hill; teach the two-level plan). T3: Tallinn grew wealthy as a HANSEATIC League trading city, and its merchants' guildhalls and spired churches survive nearly intact -- UNESCO-listed since 1997 (answer = a Hanseatic trading city). T4: Toompea's hill is a natural limestone cliff -- part of the Baltic Klint, a great pale escarpment that runs for hundreds of km along the coast, giving the upper town its natural rampart (answer = the limestone klint/escarpment; teach escarpment).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): UNESCO WHC list #822 (Historic Centre of Tallinn); Wikipedia 'Tallinn Old Town'; historyhit.com (Tallinn Old Town, 46 towers).
framing_note: Voice: place-anchored, Tallinn/Toompea named in the stem; the wonder is the near-complete survival of a whole medieval town. Accuracy rail: '46 original towers, about half surviving' -- keep the fraction honest (roughly 20-26 stand today per sources); the Baltic Klint escarpment is real geology worth teaching. Dinner-test payoff: a living medieval town whose stone wall still bristles with watchtowers (T1-T2). LANE BORDER: the Hanseatic League's TRADE/economics stays a place-identity fact here, not an economics lesson.

name: Dubrovnik
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: The walled 'Pearl of the Adriatic' on Croatia's Dalmatian coast. T1: Dubrovnik's whole old town is wrapped in a complete unbroken ring of stone SEA-WALLS -- you can walk the full circuit, roughly 1,940 m, all the way around the city above the rooftops and the sea (answer = the complete walkable city walls). T2: invert the wonder -- those walls rise up to 25 m high and up to 6 m thick on the land side, and in all their centuries no hostile army ever BREACHED them (the massive fortifications are the hook; 'never breached' the answer -- a dinner-test payoff). T2: inside the walls the main street, the Stradun, is paved end to end in white limestone polished to a glassy shine by centuries of footsteps (answer = the polished limestone Stradun). T3: the walls guarded the Republic of Ragusa, a tiny sea-trading city-state that kept its independence for centuries less by armies than by shrewd diplomacy and tribute-paying (answer = the Republic of Ragusa). T4: the whole Dalmatian coast is bright white KARST limestone -- rock dissolved and sculpted by water -- and it's that gleaming limestone against a clear blue sea that makes Dubrovnik the 'Pearl of the Adriatic' (answer = the white karst limestone coast; teach karst).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Grokipedia 'Walls of Dubrovnik'; Wikipedia 'Walls of Dubrovnik'; wallsofdubrovnik.com (dimensions, never breached); historyhit.com (Dubrovnik City Walls).
framing_note: Voice: the PLACE (the walls, the coast) is the wonder, Dubrovnik named in the stem. Accuracy rail: keep the wall figures exact (~1,940 m circuit, up to 25 m high, up to 6 m thick landward) and 'never breached by a hostile army' as the verified claim; teach 'karst' before the limestone-coast rung. Dinner-test payoff: walls that no army ever broke through (T2). A one-line modern-fame aside (Dubrovnik played King's Landing in Game of Thrones) is fine but NOT its own rung. Distractors = other real walled cities / other coastal superlatives.
history_overlap: The Republic of Ragusa's diplomacy and trade history sit adjacent to the history bank; keep this rung's answer the PLACE/polity name anchored to the walls, not a narrative of its statecraft.

name: Bergen
strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
scope: Norway's western port, the 'gateway to the fjords'. T1: Bergen sits in a natural bowl ringed by SEVEN mountains, its old harbor front lined with a row of tall, narrow, pointed wooden gable-houses -- the Bryggen wharf (answer = the seven mountains / the Bryggen waterfront). T2: Bryggen was the Hanseatic wharf -- a walled German merchant trading post (a Kontor) that ran Norway's dried-cod trade for about 400 years, and it's the last of only four such Hanseatic Kontors in Europe still standing (UNESCO-listed) (answer = the Hanseatic wharf/Kontor). T2: Bryggen has burned to the ground again and again over the centuries -- and each time the townspeople rebuilt it on the exact same medieval street plan, with the same leaning colorful gables (answer = rebuilt on the same medieval plan after every fire). T3: invert the wonder -- Bergen is the RAINIEST city in Europe, with rain falling on roughly 230 days a year; locals joke you can spot a Bergener because they never carry an umbrella, just wait it out (the extreme rain-count is the hook; 'the rainiest city' the answer -- dinner-test). T3: the rain has a cause you can see: wet Atlantic air blowing in off the sea slams into the seven mountains, is forced upward, cools, and wrings its water out right over the city (answer = the mountains force the wet air up and it rains; teach orographic rainfall). T4: the Floibanen funicular railway climbs steeply up Mount Floyen for a view over the whole city, and from Bergen's harbor boats set out into Norway's great fjords -- earning it the title 'gateway to the fjords' (answer = the funicular / fjord gateway; teach fjord).
source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Bryggen'; visitnorway.com / hurtigruten.com (Bergen, seven mountains, gateway to fjords); planetware.com (City of Seven Mountains); Floibanen (opened 1918).
framing_note: Voice: PLACE -> WONDER, Bergen/Bryggen named in each stem; invert on the rain (230 days -> rainiest city). Accuracy rail: teach 'orographic rainfall' (moist air forced up mountains, cools, rains) as the real mechanism, not just the wet-city trivia; Bryggen is 'the only Hanseatic Kontor still preserved' -- keep that precise. Dinner-test payoff: Europe's rainiest city, ~230 rainy days a year (T3). LANE BORDER: the dried COD (stockfish) is a food/animal -- name it only as the goods the Kontor traded; the answer stays the PLACE (the wharf, the trading post), never the fish's biology or the dish.
